reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Thesis: an integration lasts ten years if it depends only on a stable identifier, a normalized vocabulary and an explicit now/later line; the providers differ in where state lives

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: One Interface over Two Object Models ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's 2024 payment service puts one internal API and five states of its own over two provider adapters

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: One Interface over Two Object Models ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The Silent Webhook incident showed the cost: the adapter's read call had been leveled down to its own table, so Stripe's correct record was unreachable

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: One Interface over Two Object Models ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Femke's question for the redesign: which parts of the two models can be made identical and which difference callers must see

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Payment APIs Age: The Networks Underneath Keep Changing ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Payment methods behave differently underneath the API; cards are the exception in being immediate and needing no customer action

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Payment APIs Age: The Networks Underneath Keep Changing ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Over an integration's long life the provider's objects swell as each new method is fitted into a shape made for the first

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Payment APIs Age: The Networks Underneath Keep Changing ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Integrations break not from growth but when a difference between methods reaches code that assumed the card pattern of one call, yes or no

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Why Payment APIs Age: The Networks Underneath Keep Changing ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The author's claim: three things can stay fixed for ten years, a stable identifier, a normalized vocabulary and an explicit now/later line

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: An API either names resources you can read again (Stripe) or offers commands that return a result and leave nothing to fetch (Adyen Checkout)

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Every payment has a provider identifier and yours; Stripe's names a typed object, Adyen's names a single request, so your own reference does the grouping

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The models part on reading state: Stripe keeps it as a status field you can GET any time, Adyen gives a result code per response and then webhooks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe lets you expand related objects on request, at a stated performance cost, and its v2 paths dropped the convention

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen has no expansion; extra fields are switched on per account, so an adapter must treat each as optional

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Pagination and list consistency also vary, between Stripe's v1 and v2 and across Adyen's API families

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What an Object Model Is Made Of: Identity, State and Related Data ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: Metadata is the one field that is yours: the provider stores it uninterpreted so you can tie its objects to your records, a job Adyen's required reference does

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: An error model must keep three outcomes apart, no answer, rejected and refused, because each calls for a different retry decision

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe reports a refused card as an HTTP 4xx, so only the error type, not the status code, separates a refusal from a bad request

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen reports the same refusal as an HTTP 200 with a result code, reserving 4xx and 5xx for requests it did not accept or store

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The refusal reason comes from a list each provider maintains by mapping issuer codes; it drives retry logic and its detail is kept from the customer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: A response may be only an acknowledgment or a provisional answer, and both providers document that line / glosses dispute and settlement for the table

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Error Model, and the Line Between Now and Later ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: An API that states the now/later line is harder to start with but cheaper over ten years

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe assembles its API as one host and one object model, now in two namespaces with different conventions; payment objects remain in v1

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen's surface is several API families, each with its own version counter and conventions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen's families mix two styles: a command-shaped Checkout API and resource-shaped platform and management APIs

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Neither overall shape is free; each shifts work between provider and integrator

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The opposing view: the uniform, resource-oriented API simply wins and Adyen's variety is design debt, a view with some merit on learning cost

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Shapes for the Whole: One Resource Model or Several API Families ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Rebuttal: uniformity is not what lasted, since both providers changed conventions while the identifier, outcome vocabulary and now/later line held

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Each Company Says It Designs Its API, and Where the Record Stops ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe designed PaymentIntents by writing documentation first for every real and imagined payment method, testing the model against future methods

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Each Company Says It Designs Its API, and Where the Record Stops ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's record on reviewing API changes is thin: a mailing-list review in 2017, automated pattern checks by 2026, with the patterns unpublished

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Each Company Says It Designs Its API, and Where the Record Stops ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen's one account describes team-owned APIs with an advisory review group and a linter, which may explain its differing families

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Each Company Says It Designs Its API, and Where the Record Stops ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Both companies generate client libraries from a machine-readable specification, so library types are the object model at one version

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How Each Company Says It Designs Its API, and Where the Record Stops ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The public record stops short of design guides, review criteria and Adyen's frameworks, so the comparison is of what the APIs document, not of design quality

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces the summary table of six documented differences, with the author's inference marked as such

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The same integration is built differently on each provider, but on both you send your own reference with every payment

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: An Adapter That Hides Two Vocabularies and Shows One Difference ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's 2027 interface has four elements: own ID written first, six request outcomes, a normalized refusal reason with raw value, and a confirm call that names its source

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: An Adapter That Hides Two Vocabularies and Shows One Difference ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Worked success case on Adyen: write the row, send its ID as reference, return approved, and mark paid only when the webhook arrives

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: An Adapter That Hides Two Vocabularies and Shows One Difference ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Worked refusal case: both providers' encodings map to one refused outcome that goes to the renewal schedule, not to a transport retry

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: An Adapter That Hides Two Vocabularies and Shows One Difference ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The confirm call exposes the one allowed difference by reporting whether the state came from the provider's object, Larkfield's events or a report

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong: Lost Responses, Unknown Codes and Models That Leak ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: When a create response is lost, the row written before the request is what makes recovery possible on either provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong: Lost Responses, Unknown Codes and Models That Leak ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Vocabularies are normalized, not closed, so unknown values need a rule: store raw, change no state, do not retry, count them

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong: Lost Responses, Unknown Codes and Models That Leak ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A refusal misread as a failed request gets resent within seconds; the fix is to classify the response in the adapter before retry logic sees it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong: Lost Responses, Unknown Codes and Models That Leak ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Model conveniences fail at their documented limits, so money paths should read single objects or wait for confirmation and leave expansion and lists to the back office

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Established facts: both supply the three dependables, they encode refusals on opposite sides of HTTP success, and only Stripe's payment can be fetched

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Context-dependent judgments: the worth of a fetchable object, the burden of several families and whether to adopt Stripe's v2

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The author's position: judge a payment API by what your own system must remember, have the adapter show where state was read, and start by listing what cannot be read back

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Eight design-review questions that apply the chapter's position

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Get payment now states where its answer came from / everything here assumed a response arrived, and the next chapter starts with the timed-out request

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 50 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; the three opening callouts match no paragraph. Small omission noted, not a mismatch: the Established list (p46) leaves out the spec's item that both providers generate libraries from a published specification.

Two units were marked two_ideas. Error Model ¶5 (p23) holds one idea, answer versus acknowledgment; the dispute and settlement gloss is a misplaced aid for its table, recorded under flow. Questions to Ask ¶2 (p50) holds one idea, the hand-off; its two callback sentences are the known information the 'But' turns from.
Every unit ties to a supporting claim C1 to C5 through its section; the journey and roadmap paragraphs are declared context and transition.

results.finding: The introduction opens on a concrete puzzle, states a specific disputable claim and gives a roadmap; none of the listed patterns.
The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, adds a synthesis and a course of action, and ends on the callback and hand-off; none of the listed patterns.

The synthesis bullet says every element answers what the provider will remember and let you ask again, and that the providers differ in whether you can ask twice, which no single section states; the so-what is to judge an API by what your own system must remember and to have the adapter hide vocabularies and show the source.

The closing paragraph returns to the get payment call and says its answer now names its source. Note: the In Practice section attaches the source to a new call, confirm, so the two passages name the call differently.

The cold reader predicted every section in the roadmap's order, the three kinds of evidence (the Larkfield case, documented API behaviour, the companies' own publications) and the plain declarative tone.

The answer has the own record with own reference written before the request and the provider's identifier stored on return, later states by webhook and settlement report matched by the reference, the lost response that cannot be read back, and names the shape as Adyen's Checkout API as against a fetchable provider.

The answer gives one outcome, refused with a normalized reason and the raw value, explains both responses as a processed request the issuer declined, and says treating either as a failed request sends an answered payment again.

Each statement about design practice carries its year (2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2026) or follows from a dated post named in the same passage, and the page says 'Neither company has published its API design guide, the criteria its reviewers apply or who sits on the review.'
